easy.heading: Warming Up With My Morning Coffee
easy.body:
Today’s easy puzzle was a great way to start the day. I immediately spotted that large region covering cells [1,0], [1,1], [1,2], and [2,0]. Since it had an equals constraint, all four of those spots had to be the same number. Looking at my dominoes, the [6,6] jumped out at me. By placing the [6,6] domino at [1,0] and [1,1], I knew the other two cells in that region also had to be 6. This made it much easier to narrow down the rest of the board.

From there, I focused on the bottom left. Since cell [2,0] was now a 6, the domino covering [2,1] and [2,0] had to be the [1,6]. This worked perfectly because cell [2,1] had a less than 2 constraint, and 1 fits that bill! After that, the top left fell into place. I used the [5,6] domino for [0,2] and [1,2], and finished off the middle with the [1,5] and [2,2] dominoes. It is all about finding that one big anchor and letting the rest follow.

medium.heading: Things Are Heating Up
medium.body:
The medium puzzle took a bit more head-scratching, but it was so satisfying once the pieces clicked. I started by looking for the most restrictive spot, which was the empty constraint at cell [0,3]. In Pips, that usually means the cell has to be a zero. I paired it with the [0,4] domino, which put a 4 in cell [0,4]. Because cells [0,4] and [0,5] were part of an equals region, I knew [0,5] had to be a 4 as well.

Once I had that 4 in place, I looked at the sum of 10 in the bottom left. I had a few options, but the equals constraint at [1,3], [2,2], and [2,3] really helped narrow things down. I realized the [5,5] domino wouldn't work there, so I saved it for the larger sums. The breakthrough was realizing that cell [1,5] needed to sum to 3, which guided my placement for the [6,4] and [0,3] dominoes. It felt like a little game of tug-of-war until every domino finally found its home!

hard.heading: The Ultimate Thursday Mountain To Climb
hard.body:
Wow, the hard puzzle today was a real brain teaser! The turning point for me was the top right corner. Cell [0,6] had a sum constraint of 1, which is about as narrow as it gets. I paired it with cell [1,6] to use the [5,1] domino. This was a huge help because cells [1,6] and [2,6] had to sum to 10. Since [1,6] was now a 5, cell [2,6] also had to be a 5. I searched my list and found the [0,5] domino, which let me put a 0 in the empty cell at [3,6].

Another tricky spot was the greater than 10 region at [2,1] and [3,1]. You need two big numbers to hit a sum higher than 10, so I tried out my 5s and 6s. Placing the [6,5] domino there was the key. It took me a second attempt to get the bottom half right, especially with the equals regions at [5,4] and [6,4], but once I placed the [5,5] and [4,4] dominoes, the whole grid finally stabilized. It definitely required some patience today, but that is why we love it, right?

explanation.tips: Always start with the smallest regions or the empty constraints, as these have the fewest possible combinations. It is also really helpful to cross off your dominoes on a piece of paper as you use them so you do not accidentally try to use the [2,2] twice!
explanation.learned: Today taught me how much the empty cells can act as an anchor for the entire grid. I also noticed a neat pattern where large sums like 10 almost always force you to use your highest-value dominoes early on, which actually makes the rest of the puzzle easier to manage.

faqs.question: What does the empty constraint mean in the Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: An empty constraint means the pips in that specific cell must add up to zero. It is essentially a free zero for whatever domino you place there.

faqs.question: How do equals regions work in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: In an equals region, every single cell within that colored area must contain the same number of pips. If one cell is a 5, they all must be 5s.

faqs.question: Can I use the same domino twice in one puzzle?
faqs.answer: No, you can only use each domino from the provided list exactly once. If you find yourself needing a domino you already placed, you might have a mistake somewhere else.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for sum regions?
faqs.answer: Look at the target number and the number of cells in the region. If the sum is very high or very low, it drastically limits which dominoes can fit there.

faqs.question: Is there always a logic-based way to solve Pips?
faqs.answer: Yes! While it might feel like guessing sometimes, every Pips puzzle is designed to be solved using deduction by looking at how regions and dominoes overlap.
